title: Print, Protect & Share
goal: Print only the cells you mean with headings on every page, send a PDF, lock formulas while leaving input cells open, and share a sheet with the right people.

steps.text:
A weekly report is done, and then three things go wrong:

• The printout splits over pages and page 2 has **no headings**.
• The **Internal note** column, meant for you, prints for the customer.
• A colleague types over a formula and nobody notices.

This lesson fixes all three: **print setup**, **locking** cells and **sharing** safely.

steps.prompt:
Look **before** you print. Press [[Ctrl]] + [[P]] and Excel opens a preview of the page on the right, with the settings on the left: printer, pages, orientation, scaling and margins.

Press [[Esc]] afterwards to leave without printing anything. On a Mac, it's [[Cmd]] + [[P]].
clues: P for Print. Hold Ctrl, tap P.

steps.prompt:
The customer shouldn't get the **Internal note** column. Tell Excel what to print by selecting only the cells that should appear: from ==A1== to the last row of **Amount**. Then press [[Enter]].

In Excel you'd follow it with **Page Layout → Print Area → Set Print Area**.
steps.wrongFeedback: Select the heading row and all five days, in columns A to D only. Column E (Internal note) stays out.

steps.prompt:
The real report runs to 120 rows over three pages, and pages 2 and 3 would have numbers but no headings. **Print Titles** repeats a row at the top of every page.

Click the row number of the row with the **column headings**, then press [[Enter]].

In Excel: **Page Layout → Print Titles → Rows to repeat at top**.
steps.wrongFeedback: Repeat the **column headings** (Item, Qty, Amount) on every page, not the report title above them.
clues: The headings sit in row 2, under the big title.

steps.prompt:
A report has **121** rows and about **60** rows fit on one page. A page that's only partly full still takes a whole sheet of paper.

How many pages will it print? Type the number in ==C2== and press [[Enter]].
steps.explain: 121 divided by 60 is just over 2, so row 121 spills onto a **third** page, holding one lonely row. Spotting that in the preview is why you look before you print.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Two full pages hold 120 rows. Where does row 121 go?

steps.prompt:
The report is 8 columns wide, so column H prints alone on extra pages. You want all columns on one page width, with the rows still running on to more pages if needed.

What do you set under **Page Layout → Scale to Fit**?
steps.explain: Width 1 page squeezes the columns together while **Automatic** height lets the rows flow on normally. “Fit Sheet on One Page” would cram all 121 rows onto one tiny page.
wrongFeedback: That also fits the width, but it squeezes all 121 rows onto a single page, so the text becomes tiny.
That works by hand but you'd have to redo it whenever the data changes. Scale to Fit does it for you.
clues: You want the width squeezed, not the height.

steps.prompt: Your manager will read the report on her phone, and nobody should be able to change a number by accident. What do you send her?
options: A **PDF**: save a copy or export, and pick PDF as the file type
steps.explain: A PDF looks exactly like the print preview and opens on any phone. Set the print area, titles and scaling **first**: the PDF uses those settings.
wrongFeedback: The Excel file lets anyone edit formulas by accident, and it may look different on her phone.
A photo is blurry and cropped, and the numbers can't be copied out.
clues: Which format looks the same everywhere and isn't easy to edit?

steps.prompt:
Every cell starts **locked**, but locking only does something once you **protect the sheet**. So decide first which cells people can still type in.

Cashiers type the **Qty**; the prices and totals must stay safe. Select the Qty cells, then press [[Enter]].

In Excel: right-click, **Format Cells**, **Protection** tab, then untick **Locked**.
steps.wrongFeedback: Only the Qty cells, `C2` to `C5`, should be unlocked. Item, Price and Total stay locked.
clues: Which column do the cashiers type into?

steps.prompt:
You choose **Review → Protect Sheet** but forget to unlock the Qty cells. Sana opens the file and tries to type **3** in `C2`.

What happens?
options: It works, because Qty cells are special
Excel refuses: the sheet is protected and every cell is still locked
Excel unlocks the cell for her
steps.explain: Locked is the default for **every** cell, so Protect Sheet blocks them all, Qty included. Unlock the input cells first, then protect. If you set a password, keep it safe: Excel can't recover it for you.
wrongFeedback: Excel has no special treatment for Qty. A cell is unlocked only if **you** unlocked it.
Excel never unlocks anything on its own.

steps.prompt: The finished sheet is saved in OneDrive. Your manager only needs to **read** it. Two teammates need to **fill in** Qty at the same time. Which setup in the **Share** box is safest?
options: Manager **Can view**, teammates **Can edit**, each invited by name
Email the file to all three
steps.explain: Give each person only the access they need, and invite them by name so a forwarded link doesn't let a stranger edit. People with **Can edit** on a OneDrive file can work in it together at the same time.
wrongFeedback: That lets the manager, and anyone she forwards the link to, change your numbers.
Three copies drift apart and you end up merging them by hand.
clues: Who needs to change things, and who only needs to look?

steps.prompt:
Challenge. Ms Rao will type marks into **Maths** and **Science** for four students. **Total** is a formula and the names must never change. You're about to protect the sheet.

Select the cells that must stay **unlocked**, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Marks go into both subject columns, and nowhere else: not the names, not the Total formulas.
clues: Two columns of marks, four rows.
